name: Beta 0.46.9.214
notes: The frame-rate counter is now Performance in Settings → Graphics, and its line above the panel also shows how long each frame takes and the draw calls. About no longer shows them, so you can keep using the map while you watch.

log.t: The frame-rate counter is now Performance in Settings → Graphics, and its line above the panel also shows how long each frame takes and the draw calls. About no longer shows them, so you can keep using the map while you watch.

Settings has a new Graphics card: choose the resolution (Automatic, High, Medium or Low) and turn on a frame-rate counter above the panel. The panel no longer blurs the map behind it and is a little darker instead, which saves your phone some work on every frame.
Bases and the station now draw in far fewer steps, so the game should run more smoothly, especially on phones.
The About screen now shows how long your device takes to draw each frame, and how many draw calls it makes.
The 3D graphics now run on the latest version of their library, so everything should look and play the same; the game now needs WebGL 2, and a device without it shows a message instead of starting.
The 3D graphics now run on a newer version of their library, so everything should look and play the same; tell us if anything looks off.
The About screen now shows which graphics features your device supports.

The buttons over the map are now small round icons: tap ♪ to turn the music on or off and hold it to change the volume, which has moved out of Settings. ⌖ Recenter only appears once you've moved the view. The ▲ and ◈ icons under your credits are gone. A line under your income now says when a Market Surge is ready and, while one runs, how long it has left.
Pinching out past level 2 now hands the view back to the map, so a one-finger swipe moves the galaxy instead of turning what you were zoomed on.

Progress is slower: planets past Kallyur'Dadh mine less the further out they are, warping earns much more star dust, and the new When to warp section on the Warp tab tells you when a warp is worth it. Bonuses that barely mattered are stronger: Ore yield points add 4% each, rich veins last 5 minutes and the bigger-veins perk doubles them, and the settlement ore, ship-speed and smelting upgrades are bigger. Settlements take longer to grow (30 minutes, 2 hours and 6 hours, a little longer on later planets). The new Habitat Modules research, the Settlers perk, each full City you own and some galaxy event rewards all make them grow faster. Tapping a planet's button now steps between the three middle zoom levels (pinch still reaches the closest and widest views), and the view stays centred on the probe and other moving things instead of trailing behind them. When an update changes how the game plays, it opens with a short note on what's different, and on the web you can keep playing your current version until you next open the game.

Settlements now grow over time: each level (Outpost, Town, City) fills up over 10, 30 and 90 minutes, even while you're away. Its bonus grows as it fills, and each level lets you pick one of two upgrades. The Station and Probe chips show their names in white when nothing is waiting, instead of grey. Once you've made some progress, the game asks your browser to keep your save safe. It also reminds you to export your save if you haven't for a week, and the Your save card now says where your game is kept and when you last exported it. Planet surfaces paint much faster in big games, and zooming in sharpens a planet's surface in under a second instead of taking up to 45 seconds.

Bases fade in and out as you zoom instead of popping, and a newly claimed planet's base appears as soon as you hire its first miners. Pinching zooms in towards your fingers anywhere on the map and locks on to a planet, the station, the probe or the sun as you pinch in over it; lifting a finger mid-pinch no longer jolts the view, and the Station and Probe tab buttons now line up with the planet list.

After a pinch, tapping the selected button (or double-tapping) glides to the nearest zoom level instead of jumping all the way out, picking another planet keeps your zoom, and the ◈ probe icon zooms in to the probe again. The game runs smoother on phones and uses less battery: bases close up take about half the work to draw, the game draws less often while nothing is moving, and phones that can't keep up lower the resolution a little instead of stuttering.

Moving between planets is a slower, smoother glide, pinching zooms right in to the closest view from anywhere, and the middle zoom levels run faster. The selected chip at the top of the Planet, Station and Probe tabs is now the zoom control: tap it again to step closer, with dashes under it showing the level. The Station and Probe chips sit where the planet list does, in their tab colours. The Market keeps your ores and bars in one card, with Sell everything at the top. Missions and events you don't finish now say Unsuccessful instead of Failed.

Tap any ore tag to see which planets mine it, and tap Credits for quick tips on earning more. Mission and event goals now show their ore and credits as tags, and furnaces pick their ore from colour-coded tags, with the chosen one outlined in orange. On short phones, a new tutorial step no longer shrinks to one line while the panel is opening.
Tutorial steps now start in full, and an orange arrow shrinks or expands them when the panel is open.

A guided tour walks new players through their first three planets, pointing at what to tap, and ends with a badge in the Captain's Log once one planet is fully built. Existing players are asked once whether they'd like to take it. One-time tips explain things the first time they happen, and Settings has new Tutorial and Tips switches.
The installed web game now opens with the Fair Tap Studios logo before the title screen.

The game opens on a STAR QUARRY title screen over the nebula, and the Android app starts with the Fair Tap Studios logo. The Warp tab is tidier: the User Guide has its own section, About and the version share one card, your save and erasing it share another, and the warp explanation sits under the Warp button. The User Guide's last section is no longer cut off, and Tips and tricks no longer has a stray outline.

Each mining crew has its own World Works out in the mining field in place of the ore deposits, with machinery that comes alive at every tier. Gas giant bases skim the cloud tops until fully built, then rise on glowing lift rings, and solar panels on every world are now round. Miners are more detailed, with textured skins, heavier tools and smoother driving, and ocean and gas giant miners splash as they dive. Planets, the sun, the station and the probe have five zoom levels; double-tap to step through them, and the view glides smoothly between them. The Warp tab is regrouped under Star dust, Captain's Log and Settings, Terrestrial worlds are now called Terran, and the Speed stat is now Velocity.
New on the Warp tab: Your save lets you export your game as a save code, move it to another device, and restore backups.
Saves are safer: a damaged save is always backed up and never overwritten, and playing offline is more reliable.
Station parking: opening the Park window no longer freezes the game on big saves, and the Best parking spot card stays up to date.
Molten worlds: lava lakes are larger, with bigger crust plates and fewer cracks.
Ocean worlds: the lighthouse now stands east of the mine works pad.
Ocean worlds: the lighthouse now stands between the mine works and the habitat.
Ocean worlds: the lighthouse now stands north-west of the refinery.

Ocean worlds: the three openings in the breakwater are the same width, each centred on what passes through it, and the lighthouse now stands a little bigger on its own rocky islet north-east of the refinery.
Lava is now drawn sharp at any zoom, with a rich glowing crust and molten seams that shift and pulse, and every lava pool, lake and crater throws fountains of molten droplets.
Molten worlds: the plateaus are gone and the small lava pools are now broad lava lakes with crusted, scorched shores, bubbling and spurting all across their surface.

Solar arrays on every world are now detailed sun-tracking panels on metal poles (replacing the terrestrial leaf panels and the ocean buoys): each turns and tilts to follow the sun and lies flat at night.
Terrestrial worlds: desert dunes are painted into the sand instead of standing as 3D shapes, polar snow on the sea no longer ripples, and small stands of trees grow around the base.

Terrestrial worlds: their seas and lakes now use the ocean worlds' water exactly (colours, gloss, swell, crests and glow), the brown uplands are sandy desert with crescent dunes and rippled sand, and no trees grow on the sand.

Sideways lists (tabs, planets, furnace ores) all work the same way: the selected item is centred when you pick it, and once you scroll a list yourself it stays where you left it instead of snapping back.
The icy world hauler no longer has the block-shaped wedge on its nose: its hull now ends in a framed bow plate with two lamps.

Molten worlds: their mountain ranges now use the icy worlds' alpine shapes in basalt and ash, with one peak of each range a volcano holding a lava pool. New molten plateaus carry lava lakes, and all lava (plains, craters, plateaus) drifts, bubbles and spurts like the lava pools. Eruptions work as before.

Derelict freighters reworked: each wreck is a named ship with a story and a last log entry, modelled as a broken freighter with flickering lights, venting gas, sparks, drifting cargo and debris. Tapping it sends a salvage tug from the station to reel in the cargo, and some wrecks hold an ore crate or a navigation core worth star dust.

Events: countdowns sit on the right of the Daily and Weekly events labels, a little more space before an Elite multiplier, and the (i) by a permanent boost scrolls its record into view and turns grey again when closed.

Events: the third mission of the week turns Elite once you've accepted two (no need to complete them first). Elite rewards end with their multiplier in orange, and completed or failed missions keep their objective.
Terrestrial worlds have smaller polar caps, with a narrower band of tundra and patchy snow around them.
